title: A cache ↔ the second page load

learning.goal: Follow one request through an app with a cache, and see why the hit rate decides how fast the app feels.
learning.question: A product's price changes in the database, but the cache still holds the old page for 10 minutes. What do users see, and what could you do about it?
learning.answer: For up to 10 minutes some users see the old price, because a hit never asks the database. One option is to delete (invalidate) that cache key whenever the price is saved; another is a shorter expiry (TTL) for data that changes often — fewer stale reads, but more misses.
learning.caveat: Numbers are illustrative (2 ms for a cache like Redis, 120 ms for a slow query); real ones depend on the network and the query. On a miss the app also pays the cache lookup, which is included here. Expiry, eviction, browser/CDN caches and cache stampedes were left out.

steps.text: why is the 2nd page load so fast?
steps.say: You open a product page: slow. You open it again: instant. What changed?

steps.name: server
steps.label: cache
steps.say: Behind the app there are two places to look: a fast cache in memory and a slower database.

steps.label: GET /product/42
steps.say: The browser asks the app for product 42.

steps.label: have it?
steps.say: The app checks the cache first. It is empty: a miss.

steps.label: query
steps.say: So it asks the database, which takes about 120 ms.
Before answering, the app keeps a copy in the cache.
Next request for product 42: the copy is there. A hit.
The database is not even asked. That is the whole trick.
Real traffic is a mix of hits and misses. Move the hit rate and watch the average.
A cache is only as good as its hit rate: at 0 % it only adds work; at 90 % most users never wait for the database.
The catch: a copy can be out of date. Deciding when to throw it away is the hard part.
